title: Can the energy system withstand a more dangerous world? | Wood Mackenzie
gist: Energy Gang live episode from Climate Week NYC 2026 argues energy security, resilience and affordability have displaced abstract decarbonisation as the core of the climate debate, as Gulf infrastructure attacks, weaponised supply and AI-driven power demand create a more volatile, harder-to-finance energy system.

insights.claim: KKR managing director Neil Brown argues that attacks on Gulf energy infrastructure mark a strategic break, exposing energy systems to cheaper, more agile forms of disruption capable of outsized damage rather than just familiar market risks.
insights.speaker: Neil Brown
insights.so_what: Asymmetric low-cost attacks raise the structural risk premium on concentrated energy assets.
insights.quote: energy systems are no longer exposed only to familiar market risks, but to cheaper, more agile forms of disruption that can inflict outsized damage

insights.claim: Neil Brown credits Gulf states with real resilience through defence spending, sovereign capital and economic diversification.
insights.speaker: Neil Brown
insights.so_what: Gulf sovereign balance sheets cushion physical shocks, supporting continuity of supply and investment.

insights.claim: Neil Brown sees a durable political settlement in the Middle East as remote, implying energy markets may face a prolonged era of instability rather than a temporary shock.
insights.speaker: Neil Brown
insights.so_what: Investors should price persistent, not transitory, geopolitical volatility into oil, gas and LNG exposures.
insights.quote: the prospect of a durable settlement in the region looks remote

insights.claim: JPMorgan's Sarah Kapnick argues resilience now means the ability to keep supplying energy through geopolitical, technological and climate volatility, not merely access to fuel.
insights.speaker: Sarah Kapnick
insights.so_what: Broader resilience definition expands investable scope to grids, storage, and redundancy, not just fuel supply.
insights.quote: resilience now means more than access to fuel
insights.locator: Sarah and Anna widen the lens

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie's Anna Shpitsberg uses Ukraine's experience to argue distributed energy systems can recover faster than large centralised assets.
insights.speaker: Anna Shpitsberg
insights.so_what: Supports the case for distributed generation and storage as a security asset class.
insights.quote: distributed systems can recover faster than large centralised assets
insights.locator: Sarah and Anna widen the lens

insights.claim: Anna Shpitsberg stresses that resilience is not the same as self-sufficiency; a secure system may require domestic capacity plus strategic partnerships, industrial policy and paying for optionality.
insights.speaker: Anna Shpitsberg
insights.so_what: Pure autarky policies may be costly; partnerships and optionality are part of the security toolkit.
insights.quote: resilience is not the same as self-sufficiency
insights.locator: Sarah and Anna widen the lens

insights.claim: Building a more secure energy system requires a willingness to pay for optionality at a time when affordability pressures are already intense, creating a core policy tension.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Security premiums collide with consumer price sensitivity, raising political risk for energy policy.
insights.quote: a willingness to pay for optionality at a time when affordability pressures are already intense
insights.locator: Sarah and Anna widen the lens

insights.claim: Climate policy becomes much harder to sustain when voters no longer feel they can afford the energy transition.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Affordability backlash is a key risk to subsidy-dependent decarbonisation investments.
insights.quote: climate policy becomes much harder to sustain when voters no longer feel they can afford the transition

insights.claim: Trade policy can support domestic manufacturing but raise prices, illustrating trade-offs in a more security-focused energy system.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Tariff-driven onshoring helps domestic manufacturers but inflates project costs.

insights.claim: At Climate Week NYC 2026 the conversation kept being pulled from climate to energy security and resilience, signalling a shift in the agenda of policymakers, companies and investors.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Capital and policy priorities are rotating from decarbonisation toward security and resilience.

themes.theme: AI demand uncertainty and decentralisation risks

insights.claim: AI and data-centre growth are lifting electricity demand, but the pace of that demand, future computing efficiency and where investment should land first remain uncertain.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Demand-forecast uncertainty creates risk of over- or under-building generation and grid capacity.
insights.quote: no one is certain how fast that demand will materialise

insights.claim: Decentralisation can reduce single points of failure in energy systems but creates new cyber risks.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Distributed energy growth increases demand for grid cybersecurity.
insights.quote: decentralisation can reduce single points of failure but create new cyber risks

insights.claim: The panel argues the stakes are now whether energy systems can stay secure, investable and politically durable, not decarbonisation in the abstract.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Investability and political durability become key screens for energy-transition assets.
